newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Nature, politics battering Honduran economy.
newsitem.headline: Nature, politics battering Honduran economy.

text.p: The Honduran economy is in a precarious position as an election year looms and severe flooding has taken a toll on the country's farmland, one of the country's top economists said Monday.

Meanwhile, law-enforcement authorities on Monday gave a concrete example of the economic toll in this Central American nation, saying more and more peasants who for generations have cultivated corn and beans are now planting marijuana.
Honduras is one of the poorest countries in the hemisphere, often cited along with neighboring Nicaragua as the worst-off after Haiti.

"The year 1997 will be one of strong political campaigns, which usually presages a lot of uncertainty about the economy, on top of the flood damage in the farming areas of the north," Alcides Hernandez, president of the Association of Honduran Economists, told reporters.
Several weeks of heavy rains culminating in last week's Tropical Storm Marco have battered Honduras's prime farmland.
The country will hold elections in November 1997 to choose a new president, three vice presidents, a new legislature and new city goverments throughout the country.
"The political campaigns siphon off human resources and materials, and the (flood) damage to crops will cause a food shortage," Hernandez said.
In any event, many peasants are abandoning traditional grains for the far more lucrative crop of marijuana, exporting it to other countries in the region, authorities said.
"In some areas, we found five fields of marijuana for every one of corn," Fidel Borjas, a special anti-drug prosecutor, told reporters.
The country's chief prosecutor, Edmundo Orellana, has warned that the county may be ripe for drug cartels to infiltrate the government.
But Fernando Garcia, the government's economy minister, was a little more optimistic, saying, "The fatalists don't make history. We can move ahead."
President Carlos Roberto Reina, 70, will step down next year after four years of implementing austerity programs that he had criticized in his 1993 campaign.
Even one of his vice presidents, Guadalupe Jerezano, called on Reina to reverse course.
"I think it's necessary to reverse it," she said. "We've seen that it's not a model to pull us out of poverty."
